title: Schelling's Strategic Turn
description: Conflict as bargaining: Schelling on commitment, threats and focal points

concepts.title: War as a Bargaining Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
The game theory you met in economics grew up around zero-sum games such as chess, where one player's gain is exactly the other's loss. Thomas Schelling began to apply game-theory methods to global security and the arms race in the mid-1950s,1 and he concluded that zero-sum thinking gets war wrong. Two states on the brink share at least one interest: neither wants the catastrophe. In The Strategy of Conflict (1960) he stressed that almost all strategic situations mix conflicting and common interests, so war belongs to the theory of bargaining as much as to the theory of combat.

The shift changes the questions you ask. If both sides would rather settle than fight, what matters is how each can shape the other's expectations. Force counts for what it threatens as much as for what it destroys, and the art is to influence a rival's choices while it tries to influence yours. Schelling's recommended method was humble: draw a diagram of the options open to you and your opponent, then work through what happens in each case. The exercise also reminds you that the other side faces a decision problem much like your own.

His conclusions were often paradoxical. The 2005 Nobel announcement singled out three: a party can strengthen its position by overtly worsening its own options;2 the capability to retaliate can be more useful than the ability to resist an attack; and uncertain retaliation can be more credible and more efficient than certain retaliation. Each returns later in this topic, as commitment, as second-strike deterrence and as brinkmanship.

Schelling, born in 1921 in Oakland, California, shared that prize with Robert Aumann for having enhanced our understanding of conflict and cooperation through game-theory analysis. His books, including Arms and Influence (1966), had a profound impact on Cold War military thinkers and played a major role in establishing strategic studies as an academic field.

concepts.title: The Power of Binding Yourself
concepts.contentHtml:
Schelling's most famous paradox is that weakness can be strength. Picture a general who burns the bridges behind his own army.1 He has removed his option to retreat, and that is the point: the enemy now knows his troops will fight, so it may not attack at all. The same logic runs through ordinary bargaining. A firm may send a negotiator with limited powers to concede, and a politician may make public promises that would be embarrassing to break.

The key idea is a commitment: a move that changes your own future incentives so that a threat or promise becomes believable. Saying "I will retaliate" costs nothing, and your rival knows that when the moment comes you may prefer not to. A commitment works only if it is irreversible or can be undone only at great cost; commitments that are cheap to reverse will not win large concessions.2 Reinhard Selten later formalised Schelling's ideas about credible threats, work recognised by the 1994 economics prize.3

Schelling also separated two uses of threats. Deterrence aims to stop an opponent from doing something, such as attacking. Compellence aims to force it to do something, such as withdraw. Notice why the difference matters: a deterred state can comply simply by carrying on as before, whereas a compelled state must be seen to back down.

Commitment also explains why threatening to mobilise is not the same as mobilising. In the Nobel committee's simple model, a country that can credibly pre-commit to mobilise if, and only if, its rival mobilises deters the rival, and in equilibrium neither side mobilises at all. Commitment has a price, though. A bridge once burned cannot be rebuilt if you misjudged the enemy, and if both sides make irreversible and incompatible commitments, the result can be a harmful collision. Schelling warned that investments in deterrence can become dangerous in case of false warnings, or when a state misjudges its adversary's interests and intentions.

concepts.title: Focal Points and Tacit Bargaining
concepts.contentHtml:
Some strategic problems contain almost no conflict, only a need to coordinate. Ask two people who cannot communicate each to name a positive integer, and promise a prize only if they match. There are infinitely many equilibria, and formal theory alone cannot pick one. Yet in experiments with his students and colleagues, Schelling found that people coordinate far better than theory predicts. Most pick 1, the smallest positive integer.1 He called such conspicuous solutions focal points.

What makes a point focal is not logic but shared context: precedent, symmetry, a landmark, a round number, a common culture. Schelling insisted that you cannot deduce focality from the payoffs; you have to study people. One cannot prove, he wrote, "by purely formal deduction, that a particular joke is bound to be funny". The idea travelled far beyond strategy. It inspired the philosopher David Lewis's hypothesis that language itself arose as a convention for coordination.2

Focal points matter in war because enemies bargain tacitly, through actions rather than talks, and a limit holds only if both sides can see it. Schelling's own favourite example was the greatest of all. In his 2005 Nobel lecture he called sixty years without nuclear weapons exploded in anger "the most spectacular event of the past half century", an event that did not occur. He credited much of it to a nuclear taboo, which he treated as a convention in the strict sense, something that arises as if by agreement. Nuclear weapons are unique, he argued, partly because they are perceived as unique. Even when weapons could be built smaller in yield than the largest conventional explosives, size was no excuse from the curse: the line was all or nothing, which is what made it visible.

The taboo had to survive attempts to dissolve it. US Secretary of State John Foster Dulles saw it as a false distinction, saying in October 1953 that "somehow or other we must manage to remove the taboo from the use of these weapons".3 Schelling's comment was that tacit conventions are sometimes harder to destroy than explicit ones.

title: Nuclear Deterrence and the Second Strike
description: Denial and punishment, Wohlstetter's delicate balance, and the rise and limits of MAD

concepts.title: From Winning Wars to Averting Them
concepts.contentHtml:
Within days of Hiroshima, Bernard Brodie, a young Yale scholar who had been working as a naval theorist, set aside sea power and began a book on nuclear strategy.1 In The Absolute Weapon (1946) he wrote the passage often taken as the founding statement of deterrence theory: "Thus far the chief purpose of our military establishment has been to win wars. From now on its chief purpose must be to avert them." Deterrence means discouraging a rival from an unwanted action, such as an armed attack, by shaping its expectations of what will follow.

The classic literature, including a 1959 study by Glenn Snyder, distinguishes two routes.

  • Deterrence by denial makes the attack unlikely to succeed, for instance by deploying enough local forces to defeat an invasion.
  • Deterrence by punishment threatens severe penalties if an attack occurs, such as nuclear escalation or crippling sanctions, whatever happens on the local battlefield.

Most classic studies judge denial the more reliable.2 Forces placed directly in an aggressor's path speak loudly and clearly, while an aggressor may doubt that a defender will really carry out a punishment that also hurts the defender. Cold War Europe mixed the two. Snyder recognised as early as 1959 that US forces there were "incapable of denying any territory to the Soviets that they wish to take with full force".3 Yet they were more than a trip wire: even incomplete denial creates risks of escalation, raising the spectre of costs far beyond anything the troops themselves could inflict.

A second distinction concerns timing. General deterrence is the persistent, background effort to prevent attacks in non-crisis times, such as standing promises to defend allies. Immediate deterrence is the urgent attempt to stop a specific, imminent attack during a crisis. Most of the drama of strategic theory concerns immediate deterrence, but if deterrence works, most of its work is invisible: the attacks that were never planned.

concepts.title: The Delicate Balance of Terror
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1950s many Western leaders and writers believed that once both superpowers had thermonuclear weapons, all-out war had become nearly obsolete: two scorpions in a bottle, in Oppenheimer's simile.1 In a 1958 RAND paper, The Delicate Balance of Terror, the analyst Albert Wohlstetter attacked that comfort. "Deterrence, however, is not automatic," he wrote.2 The balance was precarious, because thermonuclear weapons give an enormous advantage to the aggressor.

His central idea was the second strike. What deters is not the number of weapons you own but the number that would survive an enemy's surprise attack and still reach their targets. Wohlstetter listed the successive hurdles a retaliatory force must clear:3

  • a stable peacetime operation within feasible budgets, without accidents or false alarms;
  • surviving the enemy's attack;
  • making and communicating the decision to retaliate;
  • reaching enemy territory with enough fuel;
  • penetrating active defences such as fighters and surface-to-air missiles;
  • destroying the target despite dispersal, shelters or evacuation.

An arsenal that looks huge on parade can fail at the second hurdle, so vulnerability became the strategist's main enemy. Wohlstetter stressed the particularly stringent conditions facing forces based close to the enemy. His argument in turn inspired Schelling's analysis of mutual distrust: a balance in which either side could disarm the other with a first strike is unstable even if neither wants war, because each fears the other will shoot first. Stability requires that striking first gains nothing.

The lesson is counter-intuitive. A secure second-strike force on your rival's side can make you safer, because a rival with nothing to fear from your first strike has no reason to launch its own in a crisis. On this logic, arms control should care less about raw numbers than about protecting each side's ability to strike back.

concepts.title: Assured Destruction and Its Rivals
concepts.contentHtml:
How much is enough? Robert McNamara, Secretary of Defense under Kennedy and Johnson, answered twice, in opposite ways. In a June 1962 speech at Ann Arbor, Michigan, he set out Counterforce/No Cities: deterrence would rest on the ability to strike the Soviet military, with attacks on cities held back as a reserve option. In February 1965 he announced Assured Destruction, aimed primarily at Soviet cities: the United States needed the capability, even after absorbing an attack, to destroy the aggressor "as a viable society".

His systems analysts turned the slogan into numbers. US forces should be able to destroy 20–25 per cent of the Soviet population and 50 per cent of its industry.1 Their studies showed sharply diminishing returns: 100 one-megaton warheads would kill about 15 per cent of the Soviet population and destroy 59 per cent of its industrial capacity, while doubling to 200 raised those figures only to 21 and 72 per cent.2 Beyond that, extra weapons bought little. The critic Donald Brennan of the Hudson Institute added the "mutual" that produced the acronym MAD; McNamara disliked the label but came to use it himself.

MAD was less a war plan than a yardstick for sizing forces. McNamara never changed the target list, his successors moved back towards counterforce,3 and the Carter administration's 1980 countervailing strategy made the return definitive. The argument has never closed. Robert Jervis, a theorist of the nuclear revolution brought by secure second-strike forces, cautioned that in a real world of imperfect control its stabilising effect, "although not trivial, is not so powerful". In 2017 Keir Lieber and Daryl Press argued that advances in technology are undermining states' ability to hide and protect their arsenals, so that nuclear deterrence is "neither automatic nor permanent".4 Their claim drew sharp replies, and whether accurate missiles and better sensing are reviving the first strike is one of the field's open questions.

title: Brinkmanship and the Stability-Instability Paradox
description: Chicken, threats that leave something to chance, and why safety at the top invites risk below

concepts.title: Chicken and the Credibility Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Two drivers race towards each other; the first to swerve is the chicken. Strategists use the game of Chicken, also known as Hawk-Dove, for crises in which each side most wants the other to back down, but mutual defiance is the worst outcome of all. The Nobel committee's illustration is a mobilisation game over a disputed patch of territory: if one country mobilises and the other refrains, the mobiliser gets its way; if both mobilise, there is war; if both refrain, the status quo holds.

Chicken has three Nash equilibria.1 In two of them exactly one side mobilises and the other gives way. In the third, a mixed equilibrium, each side randomises, so there is a positive probability that both mobilise and war breaks out.2 Which outcome will real states reach? If they share some way of coordinating, even a small asymmetry, such as one side plainly having more to gain, can make one of the pure outcomes focal. Without such a cue, the mixed equilibrium, and with it a real risk of war, is more plausible.3 The model yields one counter-intuitive result: for plausible values, the risk of war falls as the loser's payoff improves. Leaving your rival a tolerable way to back down can matter as much as limiting your rival's gains.

Nuclear weapons sharpen the dilemma. Once both sides have secure second strikes, a threat to launch an all-out nuclear attack in response to a limited provocation is a threat to commit suicide, and your opponent knows you would not choose that at the moment of decision. This is the credibility problem of nuclear deterrence: the more terrible the punishment, the less believable it is that a rational leader would ever inflict it.

Two broad answers emerged. One is to make retaliation automatic through commitment, as in the first lesson. The other, Schelling's, is subtler: do not threaten to choose disaster; threaten to create a risk of disaster that neither side fully controls.

concepts.title: The Threat That Leaves Something to Chance
concepts.contentHtml:
Schelling's answer to the credibility problem was to separate the threat from the decision. You need not convince your rival that you will deliberately start a nuclear war. You only need to convince it that, if it keeps pushing, the situation may slip out of hand.1 In the Nobel committee's summary, the best commitment is often a probability of mobilising that is less than one, because a modest chance of war may be enough to deter.2 This is the threat that leaves something to chance.

Uncertain threats have two advantages. They are easier to make credible, because the threatener's own expected cost is smaller, and they can be adjusted. Schelling's brinkmanship means stepping up the shared risk of open conflict gradually. Each step is small enough to be believable, and the rival can lower the danger at any time by relenting. A crisis becomes what Schelling called a competition in risk-taking, shaped by how much risk each side will tolerate, and the higher the stakes, the more risk a state will accept.

Think of the brink not as a sharp edge where you choose to jump but as a slope where you might slip. Mobilising, flying close to an enemy's coast and putting forces on alert all raise the odds of an accident, a misread signal or an order no one intended. That is what makes them coercive, and also what makes them dangerous. As the strategist James Johnson puts the point, under mutual assured destruction states cannot credibly threaten deliberate nuclear war, but in a crisis they can invoke threats that leave something to chance, which raises the risk of inadvertent and accidental nuclear war.3

The Cuban missile crisis, the subject of the last lesson, shows why the idea unsettles. President Kennedy estimated the probability of disaster as "between 1 out of 3 and even".4 A threat that leaves something to chance works only if the chance is genuine.

concepts.title: The Stability-Instability Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
If nuclear war is unthinkable, do smaller wars become more thinkable? As early as 1954 the military writer B. H. Liddell Hart noted that1 "to the extent that the hydrogen bomb reduces the likelihood of full-scale war, it increases the possibility of limited war pursued by widespread local aggression". Glenn Snyder gave the idea its first detailed treatment in 19612 and returned to it in a 1965 essay on the balance of power and the balance of terror. In Snyder's words, "the greater the stability of the 'strategic' balance of terror, the lower the stability of the overall balance at its lower levels of violence". This is the stability-instability paradox.

The logic is simple. If both sides are confident a crisis will never go nuclear, each can risk limited aggression, proxy wars or insurgency, trusting the other's fear of escalation to cap the fighting. Safety at the top subsidises risk below. South Asia is the standard test. For nearly three months in the summer of 1999, India and Pakistan fought the Kargil conflict,3 not long after Pakistan joined India as a nuclear power, and the fighting stayed largely contained. Many analysts read Kargil, Pakistan's reliance on proxies and the restrained Indian responses to Kargil and to the 2008 Mumbai attacks as the paradox at work.

The paradox is contested from two directions. S. Paul Kapur argues that South Asia shows almost the reverse mechanism: violence there has come from an environment in which nuclear escalation is a serious possibility if a limited confrontation spirals, so instability at the strategic level, which Cold War logic says should discourage lower-level violence, has actually promoted it.4 Others doubt that the top is ever as stable as the paradox assumes. Christopher Watterson's "brinkmanship model" treats limited aggression under the nuclear shadow as a way of manipulating the risk of nuclear war, not as a safe activity beneath a firm ceiling. Robert Jervis likewise held that the stabilising effect of nuclear stalemate cannot be taken for granted. Either way, nuclear weapons do not simply abolish war; they change where and how it is fought.

title: Fearon's Puzzle: Why Rational States Fight
description: The bargaining model: war's inefficiency, private information and fighting as learning

concepts.title: The Inefficiency Puzzle
concepts.contentHtml:
Most explanations of war list reasons states might want to fight: anarchy, shifting power, greed, fear. In 1995 James Fearon pointed out that none of these explains why they actually do, because war is costly. Whatever two states expect a war to settle, they could in principle agree to that outcome directly and keep the lives and money the war would have burned. Realist and other scholars commonly held that rational states sometimes fight because no peaceful bargain exists that both prefer.1 Fearon showed that under very broad conditions such bargains exist.2 The real puzzle is why leaders fail to find them.

The bargaining model makes this precise. Two states dispute a good worth 1, say a territory. If they fight, state A wins with probability \(p\), and each pays a cost of war, \(c_A\) and \(c_B\). A's expected value from war is \(p - c_A\); B's is \(1 - p - c_B\). Now consider a peaceful split giving A a share \(x\). A prefers it to war if \(x \ge p - c_A\), and B prefers it if \(1 - x \ge 1 - p - c_B\), that is, if \(x \le p + c_B\). Because the costs are positive, the interval between these limits is never empty. This is the bargaining range, and its width is the total cost of war.

The derivation quietly assumes three things: both sides share the same estimates of the odds and the costs, neither values a gamble above its expected value, and the good can be split at any point. Each assumption, when it fails, opens one of the routes to war in the coming concepts. Erik Gartzke offers a vivid image for the whole puzzle: imagine a poker game in which an official burns a portion of every player's holdings after each round of play.3 Players would want to settle up without delay. War is that burning torch, and explaining war means explaining why the players keep playing.

concepts.title: Private Information and the Incentive to Bluff
concepts.contentHtml:
If war is always worse than some deal, why does bargaining fail? Fearon argued that, on strictly rationalist terms, essentially just two mechanisms can do it,1 plus a third he dismissed as empirically minor. The first is private information with an incentive to misrepresent it. Each state knows things the other does not: how good its army really is, how much it cares about the issue, how much pain its public will bear. If the two sides' estimates of the odds and costs differ, each may expect more from war than the other will concede, and the bargaining range can seem to vanish.

Why not simply share the information? Because states have reasons to lie. A state that convinces its rival it is strong and resolute gets a better deal, so weak states have every reason to claim strength too, and the rival knows it. Talk is cheap, so it persuades no one. Gartzke compares this to poker: the only way to distinguish bluffing from genuine statements is to call one another to account, forcing each other to ante up through costly contests.2 Clausewitz had made the same comparison: "In the whole range of human activities, war most closely resembles a game of cards."

The cure for cheap talk is a costly signal, an action a bluffer would not be willing to take. In 1997 Fearon distinguished two kinds. Leaders can tie hands, creating costs they suffer only if they back down later, typically through public threats that domestic audiences will punish them for abandoning. Or they can sink costs, paying up front, for example by mobilising troops. In his models leaders never bluff with either kind of signal, and they do better on average by tying hands, even though tying hands creates a greater risk of war beforehand.3 In 2021 Kai Quek argued that these two are not the only general options, adding installment costs and reducible costs as further mechanisms.4

concepts.title: Fighting as a Way of Learning
concepts.contentHtml:
If uncertainty starts wars, what ends them? The bargaining model's answer is that fighting itself conveys information. As Dan Reiter put it in a 2003 survey, the model treats the initiation, prosecution, termination and consequences of war as part of a single bargaining process.1 A battle is a signal that cannot be faked: an army either holds the ridge or it does not. As results come in, the two sides' estimates converge, a bargaining range reappears and a settlement becomes possible. The view echoes a dictum of the historian Geoffrey Blainey, in The Causes of War (1973), that wars end by resolving what caused them.

Branislav Slantchev's 2003 model sharpened the story. States learn from two sources: battlefield outcomes, which they cannot manipulate, and offers made and rejected at the table, which they can. Surprisingly, in his model the negotiating behaviour carries more information than the battlefield.2 His principle of convergence says that war stops being useful once it stops revealing anything, and that a side need not believe it will lose in order to stop fighting, nor believe it will win in order to start.3

The informational view has a sobering implication, drawn out by Gartzke in 1999: war is in the error term. If wars come from variables the participants cannot observe beforehand, outside researchers cannot observe them either. We may predict which pairs of states will have crises, but which crises become wars will stay close to chance.4 Robert Powell adds a second limit: informational accounts give a poor account of prolonged conflict.5 Most interstate wars are short, and the seventy-eight wars fought between 1816 and 1985 lasted about fifteen months on average. Wars that grind on for years, long after there is much left to learn, need a different explanation, which the next lesson supplies.

title: Commitment Problems and Indivisible Stakes
description: Preventive war, first-strike fears and the debate over indivisible stakes

concepts.title: Shifting Power and Preventive War
concepts.contentHtml:
Suppose both sides know everything about each other's armies and resolve. War can still happen if they cannot trust each other's promises about the future. This is a commitment problem, Fearon's second mechanism. Agreements between states are not binding in the way contracts are, so a deal is only as good as each side's incentive to keep it later.

The classic case is preventive war. Picture a declining state facing a rising one. Today the declining state is strong enough to win a good share of the disputed stakes. In ten years it will not be, and the rising state will then demand more. The rising state would happily promise not to exploit its future strength in exchange for peace now, but the promise is not credible: once stronger, it will want to renegotiate. Facing a worse deal tomorrow, the declining state may prefer to fight today while it still can. Both would gain from a bargain that held over time; neither can commit to one.

Thucydides explained the Peloponnesian War this way. Behind the quarrels over Epidamnus and Potidaea, he judged that the growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable.1 Robert Powell generalised the mechanism in 2006. He showed that the same logic links preventive war, preemptive attacks driven by first-strike advantages, and disputes over issues that affect future bargaining power,2 such as the fate of Czechoslovakia during the Munich crisis or the Golan Heights in the 1967 Six Day War. In each case, large, rapid shifts in the distribution of power can lead to war, because no deal struck today survives the shift.

Commitment problems also explain long wars better than information does. Fighting may teach both sides who is stronger and still not end the war, if each knows that any peace would leave it exposed to the other's future power. Fearon's own account of prolonged civil wars rests on this mechanism, and civil wars do last far longer than interstate ones: seventy of the 123 civil wars that began between 1945 and 1999 lasted at least five years.3

concepts.title: First-Strike Advantages and Preemption
concepts.contentHtml:
A second commitment problem arises when attacking first pays. Schelling's illustration was domestic. You go downstairs at night, gun in hand, to investigate a noise, and come face to face with a burglar who is also armed. Even if he would prefer to leave quietly and you wish him to, there is a danger that he thinks you want to shoot, and shoots first.1 Worse, he may think that you think he wants to shoot. Neither wants a gunfight; this surprise-attack dilemma can produce one anyway.

The logic scales up. When offensive advantages are large, so that the side striking first gains a big edge, both states would like to promise not to attack, but neither can make the promise binding, because each knows the other is tempted to break it. In a crisis the fear of being hit second can push both to strike: a preemptive war that neither wanted. Powell counts this as the same mechanism as preventive war,2 since a successful first strike produces exactly the kind of large, rapid shift in power that no earlier bargain can survive.

This is why the second-strike logic of lesson two matters so much. Crisis stability depends on the absence of a first-strike advantage. If each side's retaliatory force can ride out an attack, nobody gains by striking first and the burglar's dilemma loses its force. If forces are vulnerable, every alert and every ambiguous radar return raises the incentive to go first. Wohlstetter's worry about vulnerable forces and Schelling's surprise-attack dilemma are one commitment problem seen from two angles.

The same reasoning explains why arms build-ups can feed on themselves. Two generals may both agree that war is undesirable and prepare for peace as long as each expects the other to do likewise; but if one suspects the other is preparing for war, his best response may be to prepare for war too. The idea is ancient. As Schelling noted, Xenophon had already formulated it clearly in the fourth century BC.3

concepts.title: Can Stakes Be Indivisible?
concepts.contentHtml:
Fearon's third candidate cause is issue indivisibility. The bargaining range assumes the good can be split at any point. If it cannot, a throne that only one claimant can hold for instance, the range may contain no feasible deal, and war becomes a gamble for the whole prize. Fearon himself thought this rare. In Gartzke's summary, he dismissed it as empirically trivial because states can make side payments or take other steps that allow a bargain.1 A disputed island may be indivisible, but fishing rights, cash and concessions elsewhere are not. Fearon argued that the intrinsic complexity and richness of most matters states negotiate over, together with linkages and side-payments, mean intermediate bargains will typically exist.

Critics reply that some stakes are indivisible in the minds of those who hold them. Hassner argues that sacred places are often seen as inherently indivisible, and that this perception impedes efforts to resolve disputes over them:2 you can share a holy site's car parks but not its sanctity. Goddard takes a constructivist line, arguing that indivisibility is constructed during bargaining itself, depending on how each side legitimates its claim. Land framed as the nation's historic heart becomes harder to split than the same land framed as a strategic buffer.

Powell's 2006 reply reframes the debate with an analogy from law. Parties to a contract dispute often prefer binding arbitration to an expensive court case, provided their chances are roughly the same either way; but arbitration offers little if the loser can simply refuse to abide by it. Likewise, he argued, the problem with bargaining indivisibilities is not the absence of agreements that states prefer to fighting.3 It is that they may be unable to commit to following through. On this view indivisibility is a commitment problem in disguise,4 and Fearon's three causes reduce to two: states fight because they do not know enough about each other, or because they cannot trust each other's future selves.

title: Audience Costs and the Democratic Peace
description: Do voters make threats credible, and why do democracies rarely fight each other?

concepts.title: Audience Costs: Theory and Tests
concepts.contentHtml:
How can a leader make a threat believable when talk is cheap? James Fearon's 1994 answer was the audience cost: the domestic price a leader pays for making a public threat and then backing down. He modelled a crisis as a political war of attrition in which leaders choose at each moment whether to attack, back down or escalate. The longer the public confrontation runs, the more a retreat costs at home, so escalating ties your own hands. In equilibrium, the side with the stronger domestic audience, such as a democracy, is always less likely to back down,1 and once a crisis begins, the military balance has no direct effect. Democracies, Fearon concluded, should be able to signal their intentions more credibly than authoritarian states.

For more than a decade the theory rested mainly on models. In 2007 Michael Tomz offered what he called the first direct evidence, from experiments embedded in public opinion surveys. Audience costs appeared across a wide range of conditions, grew with the level of escalation, and were especially strong among politically active citizens.2

Historians were less convinced. Jack Snyder and Erica Borghard searched post-1945 crises in 2011 and found hardly any sign of the mechanism at work in real, as opposed to simulated, crises.3 Leaders, they argued, see unambiguous threats as imprudent, and publics care more about policy substance than about consistency between words and deeds. Studies in 2012 by Marc Trachtenberg and by Alexander Downes and Todd Sechser also challenged the theory's causal story; John Mearsheimer judged that together the three pieces appear to be a devastating critique.4 Jessica Weeks added that democracies hold no monopoly: autocrats whose elites can coordinate to punish a humiliating retreat generate audience costs too, and democracies show no significant signalling advantage over most autocracies.5 Erik Gartzke and Yonatan Lupu, themselves ambivalent about the theory, replied that process tracing is much less effective at detecting audience costs than the critics believe.6 The debate remains open.

concepts.title: The Democratic Peace: Evidence and Explanations
concepts.contentHtml:
Kant argued in Toward Perpetual Peace that republics are prone to avoid war, because when the people's consent is needed they will weigh the costs they must endure: fighting, taxes, destroyed property.1 Modern political science found something narrower and stranger. Democracies are, in general, about as conflict- and war-prone as other states, yet they have rarely fought one another.2 This pattern, peace within pairs of democracies rather than peacefulness in general, is called dyadic, and it is the democratic peace, often described as one of the most striking findings in political science.

Two classic explanations compete. The normative model says democracies carry their domestic norms of compromise and cooperation abroad, so their conflicts with one another do not escalate. The structural model says that complex political mobilisation processes impose institutional constraints on democratic leaders, so two of them confronting each other find violent conflict unfeasible. Zeev Maoz and Bruce Russett tested both on data for 1946–1986 and reported in 1993 that democracy has a consistent and robust negative effect on conflict in a dyad, that both models are supported, and that the normative model is the more robust.3 Informational accounts add a third route: if audience costs let democracies signal their resolve credibly to each other, there is little room for the miscalculation that the bargaining model blames for war.

Michael Tomz and Jessica Weeks probed the public's role directly in 2013. In survey experiments in the United States and Britain, people were substantially less supportive of military strikes against democracies than against otherwise identical autocracies.4 The reason was not that they expected war against a democracy to cost more or to fail. Shared democracy changed their perceptions of threat and morality: other democracies seemed less dangerous, and attacking them seemed more wrong. That favours a normative story over a purely cost-based one.

concepts.title: The Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
The democratic peace has drawn critics from several directions, and it helps to keep their objections apart.

  • The logic does not work as claimed. In 2003 Sebastian Rosato examined each proposed causal mechanism and found them wanting. Democracies, he argued, do not reliably externalise their domestic norms or trust one another when their interests clash; elected leaders are not especially accountable to peace-loving publics; democracies are neither slow to mobilise nor incapable of surprise attack;1 and open political competition does not guarantee that a democracy reveals its resolve.
  • Something else causes it. Erik Gartzke's capitalist peace (2007) holds that economic development, capital-market integration and compatible foreign-policy interests account for the effect usually credited to regime type. After controlling for regional differences, any one of the three is enough to absorb democracy's effect in standard samples of wars and militarised disputes.2
  • The defenders reply. Michael Doyle answered that Rosato had tested the mechanisms one at a time. The persuasive core of liberal peace theory, Doyle argued, rests on three pillars, republican representation, a commitment to human rights and transnational interdependence, working together and only together.3

What is left? Even the critics mostly accept the regularity. Rosato accepted that there is certainly peace among democracies but doubted that democracy causes it,4 and Gartzke opened his own paper by calling the finding widely accepted. The live questions are causal. Is it democracy itself, or the wealth, markets and shared interests that tend to come with it? Is it norms, institutions or information? For strategic theory, the debate is a reminder that a robust correlation is not yet a mechanism, which is exactly what the bargaining model tries to supply.

title: Cuba 1962: Theory in the Crucible
description: Secret missiles, public commitments, brinkmanship at sea and the deal that ended it

concepts.title: Secrets, Signals and a Middle Course
concepts.contentHtml:
The Cuban missile crisis began as a problem of private information. In July 1962, after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and while the Kennedy administration planned Operation Mongoose, Nikita Khrushchev reached a secret agreement with Fidel Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba to deter any future invasion attempt.1 Construction began in the late summer. On 4 September, after US intelligence found evidence of a general Soviet arms build-up, President Kennedy issued a public warning against the introduction of offensive weapons into Cuba.2

Read that warning through the last lesson: Kennedy had tied his hands in public before he knew what was coming. Despite it, on 14 October a U-2 spy plane photographed sites for medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles under construction, and the images reached the White House the next day. Now Washington held information that Moscow had tried to keep from it, and each side had to guess how far the other would go.

The president's advisers split. Some, including all the Joint Chiefs of Staff, argued for an air strike followed by invasion; others favoured stern warnings.3 Kennedy chose a middle course. On 22 October he ordered a naval quarantine, a word chosen because a blockade legally implied a state of war and because it helped win the support of the Organization of American States. That evening he went on television to declare that any nuclear missile launched from Cuba would be regarded as an attack by the Soviet Union on the United States, requiring a full retaliatory response.

In bargaining terms the quarantine was a costly signal of two kinds at once. Ships at sea were a sunk cost, and a televised commitment tied the president's hands. Yet it stopped short of war. Recall the third lesson's point about the loser's payoff: a blockade, unlike an air strike, left Khrushchev a way to back down.

concepts.title: Black Saturday: Brinkmanship Beyond Control
concepts.contentHtml:
The quarantine turned the crisis into a contest of risk, and the risk was not fully in anyone's hands. The Joint Chiefs announced DEFCON 3 as the quarantine began, and US forces were later placed at DEFCON 2, meaning war involving the Strategic Air Command was imminent.1 On 24 and 25 October some Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line.

The most dangerous day was Saturday 27 October. A US U-2 reconnaissance plane was shot down over Cuba. Under the sea the danger was greater than Washington knew. On McNamara's instructions the US Navy was signalling Soviet submarines to surface with practice depth charges the size of hand grenades, and procedures for this had been sent to Moscow. No one on the US side knew that the Soviet submarines were nuclear-armed: each carried a nuclear-tipped torpedo.2 Aboard B-59, according to a later account by the communications intelligence officer Vadim Orlov, an exhausted Captain Valentin Savitsky, unable to reach Moscow, ordered the nuclear torpedo assembled for battle readiness, until the deputy brigade commander, Vasili Arkhipov, calmed him and they decided to surface. Orlov's account is controversial, and other submarine commanders doubt that such an order was given,3 but senior officers on several submarines were rattled enough to talk about firing.

None of this was brinkmanship in the textbook sense of a leader carefully dialling up a known risk. When McNamara described the depth-charge plan, Robert Kennedy recalled that those few minutes were the time of greatest worry to the President.4 Yet the gravest danger came from below the level of presidential choice: a submarine captain cut off from orders, a spy plane shot down. This is the threat that leaves something to chance in its rawest form. The risk was coercive because it was real, and real because no one fully controlled it.

concepts.title: The Secret Deal and the Limits of the Rational Actor
concepts.contentHtml:
On 26 October Khrushchev sent a long, emotional letter proposing, in effect, to remove the missiles if the United States promised not to invade Cuba. The next day a second message demanded more: the removal of US Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Kennedy decided to ignore the second message and answer the first. That night Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, secretly and indicated that the United States was planning to remove the Jupiters anyway, soon, but that this could not be part of any public resolution.1 On 28 October Khrushchev announced that the Soviet missiles would be dismantled. The Jupiters left Turkey in April 1963.2

The secret deal is audience-cost theory in reverse. Kennedy had publicly demanded the missiles' removal, so a visible trade would have looked like a retreat. Secrecy let him pay Khrushchev's price while avoiding the domestic one, and the crisis strengthened his image at home and abroad. Trachtenberg reached a related conclusion about Kennedy and Vietnam: despite strong public rhetoric, Kennedy did not see himself as locked in.3 Public words bind less than the theory assumes when leaders can concede in private.

The crisis also launched a famous critique of rational-choice analysis. In 1969 Graham Allison argued that explaining the blockade as the choice of a single rational government4 (his Model I, rational policy) misses much of what happened. Model II, organisation process, stresses organisational routines and constraints; Model III, bureaucratic politics, stresses the games and manoeuvres of the main players inside the leadership. Navy routines for surfacing submarines fit Model II better than Model I.

Two legacies followed. Because the leaders had struggled to understand each other's true intentions, the superpowers set up a direct link between the White House and the Kremlin, the Hotline,5 and both took the first steps towards a nuclear Test Ban Treaty. Rational-choice theory explains why the crisis ended in a bargain; the near misses explain why neither side wanted to bargain that way again.
